The intermediate plateau is consistent with a Hubbard-like regime where charge fluctuations are quenched, and the sharp drop is due to the crossover into the quasi long-ranged KIVC ordered phase.

## Appendix G Analytic spectral function in fluctuating moment regime

In this section we review the analytic spectral function calculations quoted in the main text. We will follow the treatment in Refs. [71, 86] for concreteness; see also Ref. [72] for a similar calculation in the Song-Bernevig model and Refs.[96, 99, 97, 98] for the development of a systematic order-by-order expansion in the parameter $s^{2}\ll 1$ .

### G.1 Small $s^{2}$ in TBG

We now review how to identify a small parameter $s^{2}\ll 1$ in TBG[71]. We begin by restating the band projected model (8)

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H} \displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{k}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}}h^{\rm sp}_{\bm{k}}c_{\bm{k}}+\hat{V}, \displaystyle\hat{V} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{q}}\overline{\rho}_{\bm{q}}V_{\bm{q}}\overline{\rho}_{-{\bm{q}}} $$

where $h^{\rm sp}_{\bm{k}}$ is the (renormalized) single particle dispersion matrix. Because the TBG bands are topological, they do not admit a symmetric localized Wannier basis. Instead, it is often convenient to work in “sublattice basis” or “Chern basis,” in which the two flat bands per spin per valley can be decomposed into a $C=+1$ and $C=-1$ band [79]. These Chern bands have most of their weight on the $A$ and $B$ sublattices respectively in valley $K$ , and vice versa in valley $K^{\prime}$ . The single particle dispersion acts as a tunneling between the two Chern sectors. In this Chern basis, the form factors $\Lambda_{{\bm{q}}}({\bm{k}})$ that enter the projected densities $\overline{\rho}_{\bm{q}}$ have an approximate $\mathrm{U}(4)\times\mathrm{U}(4)$ symmetry, originating from the strong sublattice polarization. Here each $\mathrm{U}(4)$ corresponds to spin-valley rotations in each $C=\pm$ sector. In the strong coupling limit, a large space of generalized quantum Hall ferromagnets obtained by occupying bands in the Chern basis are exact ground states at charge neutrality. Symmetry breaking terms and dispersion can be added perturbatively to split the ground state subspace, and they select the KIVC state at charge neutrality[79, 113, 114]. However, these arguments apply only to the ground state at integer filling and do not generalize to thermal states for example.

To make analytical progress for $T>0$ , and understand the extensive entropy observed experimentally[100, 101, 115], Ref. [71] introduced a small parameter $s^{2}\ll 1$ . This was done by deriving a simple ansatz for the TBG Bloch wavefunctions based on the limit of concentrated charge density at the AA sites. The resulting wavefunctions have parametrically concentrated Berry curvature and matched the TBG wavefunctions to within $\sim 5\%$ error for a fixed value of the small parameter $s\approx 0.25$ [71]. In the $\gamma=+1$ Chern sector they are given by

$$ u_{{\bm{k}},\gamma=+}({\bm{r}})=\lambda_{{\bm{k}},\gamma=+}\sum_{\bm{R}}\left(1+\frac{(z-R)/\delta}{ik/s}\right)w_{\rm AA}({\bm{r}}-\bm{R}). $$

Here $z=x+iy,k=k_{x}+ik_{y},$ and $R=R_{x}+iR_{y}$ . The vectors ${\bm{R}}$ are the moiré lattice vectors and the Bloch momentum ${\bm{k}}$ is assumed to be in the first BZ. The function $w_{AA}({\bm{r}})=\frac{e^{-\frac{\absolutevalue{\br}^{2}}{4\delta^{2}}}}{\sqrt{2\pi\delta^{2}}}\chi_{0}$ is a Gaussian peak around the ${\bm{r}}=0$ AA site, alongside a constant layer-space spinor $\chi_{0}$ that does not affect the form factors. The wavefunctions in a fixed valley and Chern sector are sublattice polarized according to the relation $\gamma_{z}=\sigma_{z}\tau_{z}$ [79]. The wavefunctions in the other Chern sector, $\gamma=-$ are related by $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ , or $u_{{\bm{k}}-}=\overline{u_{{\bm{k}}+}(-{\bm{r}})}$ . We have assumed the $\mathrm{U}(4)$ symmetry of the wavefuntions within each Chern sector due to sublattice polarization, though we allow for $h^{\rm sp}\neq 0$ .

The modulus of the prefactor $\lambda_{{\bm{k}}\gamma}$ normalizes the wavefunction while its phase defines the gauge in momentum space. Since the wavefunctions are those of a Chern band, we cannot choose a smooth and periodic gauge. We choose

$$ \lambda_{{\bm{k}}+}=\lambda_{{\bm{k}}-}=\lambda_{\bm{k}}=\frac{\absolutevalue{k}}{\sqrt{\absolutevalue{k}^{2}+2s^{2}}} $$

unless stated otherwise. This puts the gauge singularity at the $\Gamma$ point. While we can work in any gauge, Eq. (31) makes the wavefunctions $u_{{\bm{k}}}({\bm{r}})$ nearly ${\bm{k}}$ -independent for ${\bm{k}}$ away from $\Gamma$ . For such momenta, (30) resemble the wavefunctions of a trivial band consisting of exponentially localized states at the AA sites. The Berry curvature associated with the band topology is concentrated in the region $|k|\sim s$ . Our approximation uses the fact that this is a small area of phase space: $s^{2}\ll 1$ .

Wavefunctions like (30) can emerge from several types of microscopic models. Indeed a similar wavefunction appears in the topological flat bands of the Song Bernevig model as a mixed-valence hybridization of $``f"$ and $``c"$ electrons (see SI of Ref. [82]). We note that the ${\bm{k}}$ -dependence in (30) has discontinuities at the unit cell boundaries that are small in $s$ . The discontinuities originate from expanding a periodic function around each BZ center[71]. This function depends on the details of the microscopic model with concentrated charge density (e.g. the BM model). The Song Bernevig model has a similar discontunuity that depends on the UV cutoff for $c$ -electrons. For convenience, in plotting figures we replace $1/k$ in (30) with the Weierstrass zeta function $\zeta({\bm{k}})$ [116]. This choice emerges naturally if (30) are realized from a Dirac particle in a periodic and inhomogeneous magnetic field. All our conclusions will be unaffected by this choice; it only enters observables at order $s^{2}\ll 1$ and is subleading to other corrections that are $\propto s^{2}\log s^{-1}$ [71].

The Bloch wavefunctions (30) define the interacting Hamiltonian (29) through the form factors $[\Lambda_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}})]_{\alpha\beta}=\innerproduct{u_{\alpha,\bk+\bq}}{u_{\beta,\bk}}$ . These can be calculated straightforwardly by computing the requisite Gaussian integrals as in Appendix A of Ref. [71]. Due to the small phase space $s^{2}\ll 1$ , we will only need the simplified expression

$$ \displaystyle\Lambda^{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}\to*} \displaystyle=\lambda_{\bm{k}}\xi_{\bm{q}}\begin{pmatrix}1+\frac{{\overline{q}}\delta}{{\overline{k}}/s}&0\\
0&1+\frac{q\delta}{k/s}\end{pmatrix}_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}, \displaystyle\xi_{\bm{q}} \displaystyle=e^{-\frac{|q|^{2}\delta^{2}}{2}}. $$

Here we assume that $k$ is in the first BZ. We assume ${\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}$ is far from $\Gamma$ (in any BZ), which we indicate through the notation ${\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}\to*$ . We also used a compact notation $\Lambda_{\bm{q}}({\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}})=\Lambda_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}$ and will continue to do so in the next subsection.

The single particle disperion has the form[71]

$$ \displaystyle{}_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}} \displaystyle=E_{\rm BM}(1-\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2})\begin{pmatrix}0&e^{-2i\theta_{\bm{k}}}\\
e^{-2i\theta_{\bm{k}}}&0\end{pmatrix}_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}} \displaystyle+E_{\rm str}\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}[\gamma_{x}]_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}. $$

The first term comes from tuning $\theta$ away from the magic angle; it leads to the splitting $\pm E_{\rm BM}$ at the $\Gamma$ point. The second term comes from heterostrain (taken along the $x$ axis without loss of generality here) and leads to a splitting $\pm E_{\rm str}$ in most of the BZ except for the $\sim s^{2}$ area region around the $\Gamma$ point.

### G.2 Green’s function and Schwinger-Dyson Equation

We now set up notation and discuss a general identity that we will use to compute the electron spectral function. All results stated in this subsection are fully general and do not rely on $s^{2}\ll 1$ .

We will need to compute the Green’s function of more general fermionic operators $d_{\bm{k}}$ which may be multibody. We use the notation

$$ G^{d_{1}d_{2}}_{{\bm{k}},n}=(d_{1{\bm{k}}},d^{\dagger}_{2{\bm{k}}})_{n}=-\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau e^{i\omega_{n}\tau}\langle\mathcal{T}d_{1{\bm{k}}\tau}d^{\dagger}_{2{\bm{k}}}\rangle, $$

where $d_{{\bm{k}}\tau}=e^{\tau\hat{H}}d_{\bm{k}}e^{-\tau\hat{H}}$ , $\omega_{n}=2\pi(n+\frac{1}{2})$ is a fermionic Matsubara frequency, and $\mathcal{T}$ denotes imaginary time ordering. The bracket expression is useful for manipulations that rely on the linearity of $G^{d_{1}d_{2}}$ in the operators $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}^{\dagger}$ .

The electron Green’s function,

$$ G_{{\bm{k}},n}=G^{cc}_{{\bm{k}},n}=\left[i\omega_{n}-h_{\bm{k}}^{\rm sp}-\Sigma_{{\bm{k}},n}\right]^{-1}, $$

follows from the computation of the self energy $\Sigma_{{\bm{k}},n}$ . We will use a general identity for the self-energy, which we describe in detail after stating it.It has the form

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{{\bm{k}},n}=h^{\rm mf}_{{\bm{k}}}+[G^{OO}_{{\bm{k}},n}]_{\rm 1PI}. $$

The second term will be of primary importance to us. We will pause to briefly discuss the the first term, which is the frequency-independent “Hartree-Fock” contribution to the self energy:

$$ \displaystyle h^{\rm mf}_{{\bm{k}}} \displaystyle=h^{\rm H}_{{\bm{k}}}+h^{\rm F}_{\bm{k}}, \displaystyle h^{\rm H}_{\bm{k}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{G}}V_{\bm{G}}\Lambda_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}}\sum_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}\tr\Lambda_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}-{\bm{G}}}Q_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}, \displaystyle h^{\rm F}_{\bm{k}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{q}}V_{\bm{q}}\Lambda_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}Q_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\Lambda_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}},{\bm{k}}}, $$

where $Q_{\bm{k}}$ is defined through the Hartree-Fock order parameter $P_{{\bm{k}}\alpha\beta}=\frac{1}{2}(1+Q_{{\bm{k}}\alpha\beta})=\langle c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}\beta}c_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}\rangle$ . We emphasize that we do not assume a mean-field state: for a mean field state Eq. (37) describes the full self-energy.

The second term,

$$ \displaystyle{}_{\rm 1PI} \displaystyle=G^{OO}_{{\bm{k}},n}-[G^{OO}_{{\bm{k}},n}]_{\rm 1PR}, \displaystyle=G^{OO}_{{\bm{k}},n}-G^{Oc}_{{\bm{k}},n}[G^{cc}_{{\bm{k}},n}]^{-1}G^{cO}_{{\bm{k}},n}, \displaystyle O_{\bm{k}} \displaystyle=-[\hat{V},c_{\bm{k}}]=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{q}}V_{\bm{q}}\Lambda_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\{c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}},\overline{\rho}_{{\bm{q}}}\}, $$

corresponds to beyond mean field effects. The subscript 1PI (1PR) stands for one particle irreducible (reducible). The 1PR correlator corresponds to the parts of $G^{OO}$ mediated by a single-particle intermediate state, whereas the 1PI correlator subtracts off such contributions. The inverse electron Green’s function in $[G^{OO}]_{\rm 1PR}$ corrects for the double counting of the intermediate $c$ -fermion line: one from the ingoing line of $G^{Oc}$ and one from the outgoing line of $G^{cO}$ (see Ref. [71] for a pedagogical derivation of this, both perturbatively and through the 1PI effective action). The contribution (38) can therefore be understood as the contributions to the electron self-energy that are associated with scattering to strictly multi-particle states. These can then be naturally understood as the beyond mean-field contributions, as the mean-field contributions are precisely those that scatter electrons to other electrons through the mean-field potential.

We refer readers to Ref. [86] for a proof of Eq. 36, and [71] for the equivalent identity in a Hubbard-Stratonovich framework. We emphasize again that all statements above are exact. We now use small $s^{2}$ to evaluate (38) for the symmetric Mott state.

### G.3 Evaluation of Mott Self-Energy Using $s^{2}\ll 1$

To begin, we note that all diagrams contributing to the 1PI correlator (38) remain connected after cutting any internal electron line. Thus, the electron momentum ${\bm{k}}$ is always split between at least two internal lines, e.g. ${\bm{k}}-{\bm{q}}$ and ${\bm{q}}$ , with the relative momenta ${\bm{q}}$ integrated over as a loop integral. For most values of ${\bm{q}}$ , these internal lines, and the internal vertices that they connect to, have momenta far from the $O(s^{2})$ region near $\Gamma$ . Thus, to leading order in $s^{2}$ , the internal parts of diagrams contributing to the 1PI correlator (38) can be taken to be away from $\Gamma$ . For such momenta, $\hat{H}$ acts equivalently to the effective classical Hamiltonian

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}_{\rm cl} \displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{R}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{R}}h^{\rm sp}_{*}c_{\bm{R}}+\sum_{{\bm{R}},{\bm{R}}^{\prime}}U({\bm{R}}-{\bm{R}}^{\prime})\overline{n}_{\bm{R}}{\overline{n}}_{{\bm{R}}^{\prime}}, \displaystyle U({\bm{R}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{q}}V_{\bm{q}}\absolutevalue{\xi_\bq}^{2}e^{-i{\bm{q}}\cdot{\bm{R}}},\quad U(0)=U $$

which is obtained from $\hat{H}$ through $h^{\rm sp}_{\bm{k}}\to h^{\rm sp}_{*}$ and $\Lambda_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\to\Lambda_{{\bm{k}}\to*,{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}\to*}=\xi_{\bm{q}}$ . Indeed, $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{H}_{\rm cl}$ have equivalent matrix elements when all momenta are taken to be far away from the small $\Gamma$ region. See Ref. [71] for a pedagogical treatment of the above arguments, including the evaluation of simple example diagrams.

We are primarily interested with the $T\gg Us^{2}$ symmetric state with fluctuating moments, and we study the $E_{\rm str}=0$ case for simplicity. This corresponds to the Mott semimetal discussed in the main text. Nonzero $E_{\rm str}$ causes a crossover to the anisotropic semimetal, while for $T\to 0$ one should obtain a KIVC state. We comment on how these other states can be understood in small $s^{2}$ at the end. We therefore have $h^{\rm sp}_{*}=0$ , such that the flavor-moments associated with (39) are non-magnetized. Since we are also at charge neutrality, the Hartree-Fock order parameter associated to (39), which coincides with $Q_{{\bm{k}}\to*}=Q_{*}$ , vanishes. Then, to leading order in $s^{2}$ , the Hartree and Fock terms (37) vanish, as $Q\approx Q_{*}$ in most of the BZ.

We therefore need to evaluate

$$ \displaystyle{}_{\rm 1PI} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}V_{\bm{q}}\Lambda_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\xi_{\bm{q}}\,\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}V_{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}\Lambda_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}^{\prime},{\bm{k}}}\xi_{{\bm{q}}^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\left[\left(\{{\overline{n}}_{{\bm{q}}},c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\},\{{\overline{n}}_{-{\bm{q}}^{\prime}},c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}\}\right)_{n}\right]_{\rm 1PI}, $$

with $\overline{n}_{\bm{q}}=\sum_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime},\alpha}\left(c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}+{\bm{q}},\alpha}c_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime},\alpha}-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{[{\bm{q}}],0}\right)$ , where $[{\bm{q}}]$ denotes the part of ${\bm{q}}$ in the first BZ. We replaced the form factor $\Lambda_{{\bm{k}}^{\prime}+{\bm{q}},{\bm{k}}^{\prime}}$ inside the $\overline{\rho}_{\bm{q}}$ part of $O_{\bm{k}}$ with $\xi_{\bm{q}}$ since both ${\bm{k}}^{\prime}$ and ${\bm{q}}$ are summed over, and similarly for $O^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}$ . The $\Lambda_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}$ and $\Lambda_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}^{\prime},{\bm{k}}}$ factors correspond to external vertices in self-energy diagrams and are associated with the electron leaving and re-entering the small $\Gamma$ -point region respectively. As discussed above, to leading order in $s^{2}$ we can assume that no other lines or vertices depend on the small $\Gamma$ region.

It follows that we can evaluate the bracketed 1PI correlator using the classical Hamiltonian (39). For $T\ll U$ , the density matrix of (39) has frozen charge fluctuations (it is annihilated by ${\overline{n}}_{\bm{R}}=n_{\bm{R}}-4$ ) and random flavor occupations at each site. Its Green’s function is purely local, and therefore momentum independent, and takes the form

$$ \displaystyle G^{cc}_{*,n} \displaystyle=G^{cc}_{{\bm{R}},n}=G^{+}_{n}+G^{-}_{n} \displaystyle G^{\pm}_{n} \displaystyle=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{i\omega_{n}\mp U}, $$

where $G^{+}$ ( $G^{-}$ ) corresponds to electron-like (hole-like) excitations associated with creating a site with ${\overline{n}}_{\bm{R}}=+1$ $(-1)$ , thereby costing an energy $U(0)=U$ in (39). The factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ is the probability for the excitation to not be Pauli blocked. We chose zero chemical potential here since we work exactly at charge neutrality in the QMC.

The evaluation of the correlator in Eq. (40) can be similarly obtained from Fourier transforming to real space and noting that the ${\overline{n}}_{\bm{R}}$ factors sit between the fermion operators, otherwise they annihilate the density matrix, and give a positive (negative) sign for electron-like (hole-like) excitations respectively:

$$ \displaystyle\Xi_{n} \displaystyle=\left[\left(\{{\overline{n}}_{{\bm{q}}},c_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\},\{{\overline{n}}_{-{\bm{q}}^{\prime}},c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}^{\prime}}\}\right)_{n}\right]_{\rm 1PI}, \displaystyle=G^{+}_{n}+G^{-}_{n}+(G^{+}_{n}-G^{-}_{n})(G^{+}_{n}+G^{-}_{n})^{-1}(G^{+}_{n}-G^{-}_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}}. $$

The sum over ${\bm{q}}$ and ${\bm{q}}^{\prime}$ in (40) can now be evaluated. We have

$$ \frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}V_{\bm{q}}\Lambda_{{\bm{k}},{\bm{k}}+{\bm{q}}}\xi_{\bm{q}}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}V_{\bm{q}}\lambda_{\bm{k}}\absolutevalue{\xi_\bq}^{2}=\lambda_{\bm{k}}U, $$

where we used that the linear in ${\bm{q}}$ part of the form factor vanishes in the sum due to $V_{\bm{q}}=V_{-{\bm{q}}}$ and $\xi_{\bm{q}}=\xi_{-{\bm{q}}}$ . The term with the sum over ${\bm{q}}^{\prime}$ is the same. We therefore arrive at the Mott semimetal self energy,

$$ \Sigma_{{\bm{k}},n}=[G^{OO}_{{\bm{k}},n}]_{\rm 1PI}=U^{2}\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}\Xi_{n}=\frac{U^{2}\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}}{i\omega_{n}}. $$

and the resulting electron Green’s function

$$ \displaystyle G^{cc}_{{\bm{k}},n} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}-h^{\rm sp}_{\bm{k}}-\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}\frac{U^{2}}{i\omega_{n}}} \displaystyle=\frac{P_{+}}{i\omega_{n}-E_{\rm BM}(1-\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2})-\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}\frac{U^{2}}{i\omega_{n}}} \displaystyle+\frac{P_{-}}{i\omega_{n}+E_{\rm BM}(1-\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2})-\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}\frac{U^{2}}{i\omega_{n}}}, $$

where $P_{+}$ and $P_{-}$ project onto the positive and negative energy bands of $h^{\rm sp}_{\bm{k}}$ respectively (with $E_{\rm str}=0$ ). For each BM band there are two quasiparticle branches, associated with the quadratic equations $\omega(\omega\mp E_{\rm BM}(1-\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}))=\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}U^{2}$ . While the branches converge as ${\bm{k}}\to*$ , for ${\bm{k}}\to 0$ one has $\omega\to E_{\rm BM}$ while the other has $\omega\to 0$ . The branch with $\omega\to 0$ has zero quasiparticle residue at ${\bm{k}}=0$ because the self-energy pole causes the Green’s function to vanish at zero frequency. These features can be seen in the Mott Semimetal spectral lines plotted in the main text and are consistent with the QMC spectra that they are plotted with (for twist angles not too far from the magic angle).

The vanishing quasiparticle residue is suggestive of an excitation orthogonal to the electron that mixes with the electron for nonzero ${\bm{k}}$ . In Ref. [86] (see also Refs. [95, 83] for treatments using an ancilla model) it was shown that this excitation can be created through a relatively simple “trion” operator, $F_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}=\sum_{\bm{R}}\{c_{{\bm{R}}\alpha},{\overline{n}}_{\bm{R}}\}e^{-i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}$ . The Green’s function in the full electron-trion space is

$$ \mathcal{G}^{-1}_{{\bm{k}},n}=\omega-\begin{pmatrix}h^{\rm sp}_{\bm{k}}&U\lambda_{\bm{k}}\\
U\lambda_{\bm{k}}&0\end{pmatrix}, $$

where the off-diagonal terms correspond to electron-trion tunneling. Projecting (46) onto the electron degree of freedom $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}^{T}$ consistently recovers the electron Green’s function (45).

### G.4 Anisotropic semimetal and KIVC Insulator

We close by commenting on the anisotropic semimetal and KIVC states. For $E_{\rm str}$ nonzero, one obtains a crossover[86] between the Mott semimetal ( $E_{\rm str}\ll T$ ) and the anisotropic semimetal ( $E_{\rm str}\gg T$ ). The crossover is driven by the magnetization of the $\gamma_{x}$ moments in (39). The anisotropic semimetal obtained from $E_{\rm str}\gg T$ and $s^{2}\ll 1$ is a Slater determinant with $Q_{*}=-\gamma_{x}$ and dispersion $\Sigma_{{\bm{k}},n}=h^{\rm F}_{\bm{k}}=U\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}\gamma_{x}$ (the 1PI correlator vanishes for $Q_{*}^{2}=1$ ). This leads to a quadratic band touching at $\Gamma$ for $E_{\rm BM}=0$ and two Dirac cones near $\Gamma$ for $E_{\rm BM}\neq 0$ .

The KIVC state at $T\ll Us^{2}$ requires going to higher order in $s^{2}$ and accounting for exchange interactions $\propto Us^{2}$ [71]. Its emergence can be understood at a high level by adding a mean-field exchange proportional to the KIVC order parameter[79] by hand: $h_{\rm KIVC}\sim Us^{2}\eta_{x}\gamma_{z}$ , where $\eta_{x}$ flips valley but not Chern sector. For $T\ll Us^{2}$ this is sufficient to fully magnetize the flavor moments of (39) and give $Q_{*}=\eta_{x}\gamma_{z}$ . This $Q_{*}$ in turn generates a gapped dispersion through $\Sigma_{{\bm{k}},n}=h^{\rm F}_{\bm{k}}=U\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2}+U_{\Gamma}(1-\absolutevalue{\lambda_\bk}^{2})$ , where

$$ U_{\Gamma}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{q}}V_{\bm{q}}\absolutevalue{\xi_\bq}^{2}(\tfrac{1}{2}\absolutevalue{q}^{2}\delta^{2}) $$

is the energy scale associated with exchange interactions between the $\Gamma$ point and the rest of the BZ (or the $c$ -electron orbital and the $f$ -electron orbital in the Song-Bernevig basis[82]). For $V_{\bm{q}}\propto|q|^{-1}$ we have $U_{\Gamma}=\frac{U}{4}$ . We saw above that these exchange interactions, generated from the $q$ -linear parts of the form factor (32), destructively interfere for the inter-Chern nematic semimetal state and the flavor-incoherenent Mott semimetal, such that they do not generate a gap at $\Gamma$ for these states.

# Trion Excitations in Twisted Bilayer Graphene: A Quantum Monte Carlo Study

**Authors:** Shibo Shan Affiliation: Department of Physics and HK Institute of Quantum Science & Technology, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong SAR, China Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Optical Quantum Materials, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong SAR, China Cheng Huang Affiliation: Department of Physics and HK Institute of Quantum Science & Technology, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong SAR, China Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Optical Quantum Materials, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong SAR, China Patrick Ledwith Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Zi Yang Meng Email: zymeng@hku.hk Affiliation: Department of Physics and HK Institute of Quantum Science & Technology, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong SAR, China Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Optical Quantum Materials, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong SAR, China

## Abstract

Determining the nature of charge carriers is a fundamental goal in the study of strongly correlated electron systems. Here, we employ the continuous-field momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo method to reveal exotic "Dirac trion" excitations in the finite-temperature normal state of twisted bilayer graphene. While the ground state is a symmetry-breaking insulator with gapped ( $\sim$ 20 meV) electron-like excitations, we show that a small temperature ( $\sim$ 3 meV), well below the interaction scale, drives the system into a strongly fluctuating symmetric normal state. We demonstrate that this normal state hosts gapless excitations consisting of three-particle bound states, two electrons and one hole, that are exactly orthogonal to the higher-energy electrons at the zero-momentum gapless point. These Dirac trions have the remarkable property of being arbitrarily light despite being composed of heavy constituents, and their spectra can be easily tuned by varying the twist angle and interlayer hopping strength. Our unbiased quantum many-body computation sheds light on the Dirac trions in a projected correlated flat-band setting and opens the door for further investigation of many-body excitations in strongly correlated topological bands beyond Landau levels.

Introduction.- A central goal in condensed matter physics is characterizing the nature of collective excitations in strongly interacting electron systems. An understanding of charged excitations is especially important as they form the basis of doped phases. Moiré materials, such as twisted bilayer graphene[57, 11, 5, 70, 53] (TBG), introduce a new setting for strong correlations: narrow topological bands which, unlike Landau levels, can have inhomogeneous charge density in real space and inhomogeneous quantum geometry in momentum space. Thus far, significant progress has been made in showing that quantum Hall physics can be recovered in such bands [90, 54, 4, 81, 103, 108, 78, 13, 111, 104, 58, 24, 20, 67, 26, 29, 75, 66] despite these deformations from traditional Landau levels [45, 54, 97, 51, 99, 25, 98, 56, 64, 37]. On the other hand, TBG additionally hosts phenomena conventionally associated with Mott physics, such as unconventional superconductivity bordering a correlated insulator [16, 17, 109, 65, 91, 84, 6, 63, 71, 7, 92, 76, 47, 49, 69, 46] as well as large, $O(k_{B})$ , magnetic entropy per site [83, 85, 115]. Under the circumstances, one would like to ask: what new phenomena can emerge from this interplay between quantum Hall and Mott physics and, more broadly, topological bands far from the homogeneous Landau level limit?

Here we apply state-of-the-art continuous field momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) [113, 33, 112, 40, 39, 38] to the interacting narrow bands of the Bistritzer-MacDonald (BM) model [11] of twisted bilayer graphene at charge neutrality. We focus on the exotic finite-temperature normal state, which emerges from the Kramers’ intervalley coherent (KIVC) insulator ground state [12, 60, 94, 53, 22, 61, 33, 73, 106, 79, 89, 77, 86, 48] above a small temperature scale (much smaller than the interaction scale). This normal state has nearly decoupled flavor moments and, almost everywhere in the Brillouin zone, gapped charge. The $\Gamma$ point of the Brillouin zone, where the Berry curvature of the band is highly concentrated, however, hosts gapless charged excitations. This “Mott semimetal” spectrum[52] is consistent with prior numerical [33, 74, 40, 32, 14, 23, 80, 15, 34] and analytic [52, 55, 36, 50, 116, 117, 96, 35, 102, 68] studies of the TBG normal state.

We show that the lowest-energy charged excitations of the Mott semimetal are “Dirac trions:” exotic three-particle bound states that emerge from the interplay between strong interactions and concentrated band topology [55]. To do so, we compute the appropriate trion Green’s function in QMC. As will be shown below, the trion operator contains 3 fermion operators, the trion Green’s function is a six-fermion correlator whose direct momentum-space evaluation scales as $O(N^{4})$ . (more than the QMC update itself $O(N^{3})$ with $N$ the system size). We overcome this prohibitive scaling through the use of a real-space representation of the topological flat bands, which simplifies the complexity to $O(N^{2})$ (see below) and demonstrates a concrete and computationally useful application of recently developed real-space approaches to topological bands [110, 41, 31, 59, 107, 72, 52, 55, 18, 28, 9, 10, 95].

We find that the trion spectrum has a zero-energy band touching at $\Gamma$ , and verify that the $\Gamma$ point trion is exactly orthogonal to the electron as enforced by the band topology [55]. In contrast, electrons at $\Gamma$ are split by the single particle dispersion. Exactly at the magic angle, this splitting vanishes and electron and trion are both gapless. We find that the trion near $\Gamma$ is very light, despite the fact that its constituent electrons and holes are heavy. We discuss how these features emerge from an analytic theory based on the limit of highly concentrated charge density (Fig. 1 (a)) and Berry curvature (Fig. 1 (b)) [52, 55]. Finally, we comment on implications for twisted bilayer graphene experiments and future applications of the QMC method we develop.

*Figure 1: Charge density and Berry curvature of the moiré flat bands. (a) Real-space charge density $\rho(\mathbf{r})\ell^{2}$ of the two flat bands, with $\ell=\sqrt{A_{M}/(2\pi)}$ and $A_{M}$ the moiré unit-cell area. The black hexagon marks one moiré unit cell and the AA region is indicated. (b) Momentum-space Berry curvature $\Omega(\mathbf{k})/\ell^{2}$ of the $+1$ Chern band in the moiré Brillouin zone. The parameters are $u_{0}=80\,{\rm meV}$ , $u_{1}=110\,{\rm meV}$ , and $\theta=1.08^{\circ}$ .*

*Figure 2: Electron-trion hybridization and spectral function. All data are obtained at $u_{0}=80\,{\rm meV}$ , $T=3.5\,{\rm meV}$ , and $\theta=1.16^{\circ}$ . (a) Schematic analogy between the electron-trion problem and Bernal bilayer graphene, where one views the two electrons and two trions as the four sites in one unit cell of Bernal bilayer graphene. (b) Corresponding schematic band structure, with blue and orange denoting electron-like and trion-like bands, respectively. (c) BM model single-particle dispersion $h^{BM}({\mathbf{k}})$ along the high symmetry path $K-M-\Gamma-M-K^{\prime}$ . For $\theta=1.16^{\circ}$ , the BM bands have a finite single-particle splitting near the $\Gamma$ point. (d) Magnitude of the off-diagonal inverse-Green’s-function component, $|\Sigma^{cF}_{{\mathbf{k}},l}|$ , along the same momentum path with $L=15$ . The legend labels $l$ denote the fermionic Matsubara-frequency index, $\omega_{l}=(2l+1)\pi T$ . The data show that $|\Sigma^{cF}_{{\mathbf{k}},l}|\approx|{\mathbf{k}}|$ for small $|{\mathbf{k}}|$ around $\Gamma$ . (e,f) Electron and trion spectral functions with $L=15$ . The $\Delta_{sp}$ markers in (b,c,e) indicate the same single-particle gap at $\Gamma$ .*

Models and Observables.- The kinetic part of our Hamiltonian is taken from the BM model [11, 39] with $u_{1}=110$ meV, $\frac{\hbar v_{F}}{\sqrt{3}a}=2377.45$ meV and various $u_{0}$ , where $u_{0}$ and $u_{1}$ are the AA and AB/BA hopping strengths, respectively, $v_{F}$ is the Fermi velocity and $a=1.42$ Å the carbon-carbon distance in graphene. Since the gap separating the two flat bands from the remote bands is much larger than the interaction scale [105], we study the projected interaction Hamiltonian of the two bands

$$ H=\sum_{{\mathbf{k}}ns\eta}h^{BM}_{n\eta}({\mathbf{k}})c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}ns\eta}c_{{\mathbf{k}}ns\eta}+\frac{1}{2\Omega}\sum_{{\mathbf{Q}}}V({\mathbf{Q}})\delta\rho_{-{\mathbf{Q}}}\delta\rho_{{\mathbf{Q}}}, $$

where $\Omega$ is the sample area, $h^{BM}_{n\eta}({\mathbf{k}})$ are the band energies [11], and ${\mathbf{k}}$ , $n=\pm 1$ , $s=\uparrow,\downarrow$ , $\eta=\pm$ label moiré Brillouin zone (mBZ) momentum, band, spin, and valley respectively. The projected density operator $\delta\rho_{\mathbf{Q}}$ , at momentum $\mathbf{Q}={\mathbf{q}}+{\mathbf{G}}$ , is $\delta\rho_{{\mathbf{Q}}}=\sum_{{\mathbf{k}},m,n,s,\eta}\lambda^{\eta}_{mn}\left({\mathbf{k}},{\mathbf{k}}+{\mathbf{Q}}\right)\left(c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}ms\eta}c_{{\mathbf{k}}+{\mathbf{q}},ns\eta}-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{{\mathbf{q}},\mathbf{0}}\delta_{m,n}\right)$ , where ${\mathbf{q}}$ is in the mBZ and ${\mathbf{G}}$ is a reciprocal lattice vector. The form factor $\lambda_{mn}^{\eta}({\mathbf{k}},{\mathbf{k}}+{\mathbf{Q}})=\langle u_{m\eta}({\mathbf{k}})|u_{n\eta}({\mathbf{k}}+{\mathbf{Q}})\rangle$ is obtained from the BM Hamiltonian eigenstate $|u_{n\eta}({\mathbf{k}})\rangle$ . We use the long-range single-gate screened Coulomb interaction $V({\mathbf{Q}})=\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon}\int d^{2}{\mathbf{r}}\left(\frac{1}{{\mathbf{r}}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\mathbf{r}}^{2}+d^{2}}}\right)\mathrm{e}^{i{\mathbf{Q}}\cdot{\mathbf{r}}}=e^{2}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-|{\mathbf{Q}}|d}\right)/\left(2\epsilon|{\mathbf{Q}}|\right)$ , with permittivity $\epsilon=7\epsilon_{0}$ , gate distance $d/2=20$ nm [62]. As shown in our previous work [74, 73], we can cut off ${\mathbf{Q}}$ at a distance of order the moiré reciprocal lattice scale.

Following Ref. [55], we define the trion operator as

$$ F_{\mathbf{k}\sigma s\eta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{R}}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\bigl\{c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta},\,\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}\bigr\}, $$

where $c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in{\rm mBZ}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}c_{\mathbf{k}\sigma s\eta}$ and $\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}=\sum_{\sigma,s,\eta}c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}-4.$ Here $\mathbf{R}$ labels moiré unit cells and $\sigma=\pm$ labels the sublattice-polarized (Chern) basis within the two projected BM flat bands [12, 53]. This basis is related to the BM band basis by $c_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}=\sum_{n}X_{\sigma n}^{\eta}({\mathbf{k}})c_{{\mathbf{k}}ns\eta}^{\dagger}$ . The matrix $X^{\eta}({\mathbf{k}})$ is chosen such that $c_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}$ creates an AA-centered Wannier orbital with power law tails enforced by band topology [59, 52]. Thus $\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}$ represents the corresponding local charge fluctuation, and $F_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma s\eta}=\{c_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma s\eta},\delta n_{{\mathbf{R}}}\}$ is the analog of a local atomic-limit Hubbard trion [42]. At charge neutrality, the trion operator satisfies $\langle\{F_{{\mathbf{k}}},c_{\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}\}\rangle=0$ . In this Chern basis, the single-particle term in the Hamiltonian reads $\sum_{{\mathbf{k}},s,\eta,\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}[h_{{\mathbf{k}}}^{sp}]^{\eta}_{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma_{1}s\eta}c_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma_{2}s\eta}$ , where $[h^{sp}_{{\mathbf{k}}}]^{\eta}_{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}=\sum_{n}X^{\eta*}_{\sigma_{1}n}({\mathbf{k}})h^{BM}_{n\eta}({\mathbf{k}})X_{\sigma_{2}n}^{\eta}({\mathbf{k}})$ . Details of this basis construction are given in the Supplemental Material (SM) [3].

We define the inverse Green’s function in each spin $s$ and valley $\eta$ in the electron-trion space with the basis $(c_{{\mathbf{k}}+},c_{{\mathbf{k}}-},F_{{\mathbf{k}}+},F_{{\mathbf{k}}-})_{s\eta}$ as

$$ \mathcal{G}^{-1}({\mathbf{k}},i\omega_{l})=\begin{pmatrix}G_{cc}({\mathbf{k}},i\omega_{l})&G_{cF}({\mathbf{k}},i\omega_{l})\\
G_{Fc}({\mathbf{k}},i\omega_{l})&G_{FF}({\mathbf{k}},i\omega_{l})\end{pmatrix}^{-1} $$

where $G_{AB}({\mathbf{k}},i\omega_{l})=\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau e^{i\omega_{l}\tau}G_{AB}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)$ and $[G_{AB}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)]_{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}=-\langle A_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma_{1}}(\tau)B_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma_{2}}^{\dagger}(0)\rangle$ . Here $\omega_{l}=(2l+1)\pi T$ are the Matsubara frequencies, $A,B=c$ or $F$ for electron and trion respectively, and $\beta=1/T$ . The spin and valley indices $s$ and $\eta$ are suppressed for notational simplicity.

We pause to discuss an analytic theory based on the concentration of charge density (Fig. 1(a)) and Berry curvature (Fig. 1 (b)) of the TBG flat bands [52, 55]. These features underscore the strong deformation of the TBG bands away from the homogeneous Landau-level-like limit and are responsible for the Mott-like physics of the system. The theory is tractable due to a small parameter, $s^{2}\ll 1$ , where $s$ is the width of the Berry curvature distribution [52, 55, 68] (see also recent generalizations to the topological heavy fermion model [36, 96, 35, 102]) within the Mott regime $U\gg T\gg Us^{2}$ of mostly frozen charge and thermal flavor moments. This yields

$$ \mathcal{G}^{-1}({\mathbf{k}},i\omega_{l})=i\omega_{l}-\begin{pmatrix}0&h_{{\mathbf{k}}+-}^{sp}&\Sigma_{{\mathbf{k}}}&0\\
h_{{\mathbf{k}}-+}^{sp}&0&0&\Sigma_{{\mathbf{k}}}^{*}\\
\Sigma_{{\mathbf{k}}}^{*}&0&0&0\\
0&\Sigma_{\mathbf{k}}&0&0\end{pmatrix}-\tilde{\Sigma} $$

as the form of the inverse Green’s function. The second term should be understood as an effective Hamiltonian for electrons and trions. The $\Sigma_{\mathbf{k}}$ terms arise from the Hubbard-like part of the projected Coulomb interactions: these on-site four fermion terms tunnel electrons into three-particle trions and back [42, 55]. Band topology requires the phase of $\Sigma_{\mathbf{k}}$ to wind by $2\pi$ around the mBZ 11 1 The electron operator winds by $\pm 2\pi$ around the mBZ in any smooth gauge due to the $C=\pm$ band topology. The trion operator, however, is globally defined and periodic such that it does not wind. Their hybridization must therefore wind by $\pm 2\pi$ .. This requires a vortex, $\Sigma_{\mathbf{k}}\propto k_{x}+ik_{y}$ , pinned to $\Gamma$ by symmetry, where the electron-trion hybridization must vanish. In the absence of single particle dispersion, this corresponds to an electron-trion Dirac cone in each Chern sector. Nonzero $h^{\rm sp}$ couples electrons in the two Chern sectors in a similar manner to the interlayer tunneling of Bernal bilayer graphene, as depicted in Fig. 2(a), resulting in a zero energy quadratic band touching for trions. Additional contributions to the self energy $\tilde{\Sigma}$ , suppressed by $s^{2}$ , are present and contribute to broadening. The orthogonality between the electron and trion at $\Gamma$ , and the fact that the trion operator creates the lowest energy charged excitation, are expected to be robust to such corrections.

We confirm this picture with QMC simulations, described in detail below. The electron-trion hybridization, $\Sigma^{cF}_{{\mathbf{k}},l}=-[\mathcal{G}^{-1}_{{\mathbf{k}},l}]^{cF}_{\sigma\sigma}$ is plotted in Fig. 2(d); it vanishes near $\Gamma$ and approaches the Mott gap in the rest of the mBZ. The electron spectral function, Fig. 2(e), features two peaks, split by the single-particle dispersion, whereas the trion spectral function, Fig. 2(f), is sharply peaked at zero energy.

Methods.- We solve the Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) and measure the observables in Eq. (3) with the continuous field momentum-space QMC method [113, 33, 39, 38]. In the QMC simulation, we discretize the mBZ into an $N=L\times L$ momentum grid for ${\mathbf{k}}$ , with linear size $L=6,9,12,15$ . Our method employs the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA) [39, 27, 100, 21] with global updates (see SM [3]). For the long-range Coulomb interaction in Eq. (1), conventional local updates increase the cost from $O(\beta N^{3})$ to at least $O(\beta N^{4})$ . In contrast, our global-update scheme simultaneously updates all auxiliary fields on each time slice and retains the $O(\beta N^{3})$ scaling. The resulting low autocorrelation also enables efficient measurement of the six-fermion trion Green’s function.

In the QMC, we compute the two-point Green’s functions $G_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}n_{1};{\mathbf{k}}_{2}n_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=\langle\mathcal{T}_{\tau}c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}n_{1}s\eta}(\tau_{1})c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}_{2}n_{2}s\eta}(\tau_{2})\rangle$ and other observables are then evaluated as combinations of these Green’s functions through Wick expansion for each auxiliary field configuration. However, a direct momentum-space measurement for $G_{FF}$ is inefficient: since $F_{\mathbf{k}\sigma s\eta}$ contains 3 ${\mathbf{R}}$ -space fermion operators, the correlator involves 6 fermion operators and 4 independent momentum summations, giving an $O(N^{4})$ measurement cost for each $(\mathbf{k},\tau)$ , which is $O(N)$ times more costly than the QMC update. Such a naive measurement would become the bottleneck of the simulation.

To reduce the measurement cost, we avoid the problem of performing the Wick expansion directly in momentum space. Instead, after the rotation to the Chern basis, we Fourier transform the Green’s functions to the real-space moiré basis, $G_{\mathbf{R}_{1}\sigma_{1};\mathbf{R}_{2}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ , using fast Fourier transforms with cost $O(N^{2}\log N)$ . The observable $G_{FF}$ is then evaluated through Wick expansion in terms of real-space Green’s functions, with only 2 real-space summations over $\mathbf{R}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{R}_{2}$ instead of the 4 momentum-space sums, reducing the subsequent measurement complexity to $O(N^{2})$ . Further details are given in SM [3].

Spectral functions of both electron and trion are then obtained from $[G_{cc}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)]_{\sigma\sigma}$ and $[G_{FF}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)]_{\sigma\sigma}$ via the stochastic analytic continuation (SAC) [87, 8, 88]. Such a QMC+SAC scheme has been successfully applied in previous momentum-space QMC simulations to reveal the ground state and finite-temperature single-particle and collective excitation spectra of TBG [73, 114, 40, 74, 39].

Results.- At $\theta=1.08^{\circ}$ and $\nu=0$ , the ground state of Eq. (1) is known to be the KIVC insulator [12, 22, 53, 61, 33, 73] with order parameter $O_{\mathrm{KIVC}}({\mathbf{q}})\equiv\sum_{{\mathbf{k}},s}c_{{\mathbf{k}}+{\mathbf{q}},s}^{\dagger}\,\tau_{x}n_{y}\,c_{{\mathbf{k}},s}$ . Here $c_{{\mathbf{k}},s}$ denotes the spinor in valley and band space, $\tau_{x}$ and $n_{y}$ are the Pauli matrices that act in the valley space and the two-flat-band space, respectively. In the finite-size QMC simulations, the valley U(1) symmetry is not broken, and we need to compute the correlation function of the KIVC order, $S_{\mathrm{KIVC}}({\mathbf{q}})=\langle{O_{\mathrm{KIVC}}({\mathbf{q}})}^{\dagger}O_{\mathrm{KIVC}}(-{\mathbf{q}})\rangle/N^{2}$ , at its ordered wavevector ${\mathbf{q}}=\Gamma$ , to monitor the strength of the KIVC order.

Fig. 3 (a) shows how the KIVC order melts with increasing temperature. For $L=6,9$ systems, $S_{\text{KIVC}}$ vanishes quickly as $T>1$ meV. As the KIVC order breaks a continuous symmetry, it only has algebraic order at any $T>0$ in the thermodynamic limit. However, the electronic spectra of a fluctuating KIVC order with sufficiently large correlation length should be similar to the $T=0$ ordered state; hence, we observe the Mott semimetal to emerge when the flavor moment correlations are short-ranged or absent (such as $T>1$ meV here).

To detect the Mott semimetal state, we also monitor the temperature dependence of the static trion correlation function $S_{\text{trion}}(\Gamma)=\langle\{F_{\Gamma\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger},F_{\Gamma\sigma s\eta}\}\rangle$ . As shown in Fig. 3 (a), trion spectral weight at $\Gamma$ vanishes as $T\to 0$ , where the KIVC order becomes long ranged, but becomes $\approx 1$ as the KIVC correlations become negligible in the Mott regime.

The corresponding spectral evolution with temperature at $\theta=1.08^{\circ}$ is shown in Fig. 3 (c-f). At $T=0.5$ meV, inside the KIVC regime, the electron spectrum is fully gapped, whereas the trion spectrum follows a similar dispersion away from $\Gamma$ but carries nearly zero spectral weight at $\Gamma$ . At $T=3$ meV, after the KIVC correlations have been strongly suppressed, the trion spectral weight is strongly enhanced at $\Gamma$ , and both the electron and trion spectra develop gapless Dirac cones centered at $\Gamma$ . The Dirac character is further supported by Fig. 3 (b), which shows that the magnitude of electron-trion hybridization $\Sigma^{cF}_{{\mathbf{k}},l}=-[\mathcal{G}^{-1}_{k,l}({\mathbf{k}},i\omega_{l})]_{\sigma\sigma}^{cF}$ vanishes linearly on approaching $\Gamma$ with only weak Matsubara-frequency dependence, $|\Sigma^{cF}_{{\mathbf{k}},l}|\propto|{\mathbf{k}}|$ , consistent with the expected form $\Sigma_{{\mathbf{k}}}\sim k_{x}+ik_{y}$ . Figure. 3(f) therefore provides the first manifestation of the Dirac trion in a realistic and unbiased quantum many-body setting.

To further enhance the contrast between $A_{e}(\mathbf{k},\omega)$ and $A_{t}(\mathbf{k},\omega)$ , we tune the twist angle a bit away from the magic angle from $\theta=1.08^{\circ}$ to $1.16^{\circ}$ at $T=3.5$ meV. At $\theta=1.16^{\circ}$ , the BM dispersion has a finite single-particle gap $\Delta_{sp}$ at $\Gamma$ , as shown in Fig. 2 (c). Consequently, the electron spectral function retains this gap in Fig. 2 (e), in agreement with the analytic theory in Eq. (4). In contrast, the trion spectrum remains gapless and sharply peaked at $\omega=0$ meV.

We further test the role of concentrated band topology by varying the interlayer AA hopping strength $u_{0}$ at fixed $\theta=1.08^{\circ}$ and $T=3$ meV. As $u_{0}$ is increased from the chiral limit ( $u_{0}=0$ ) toward the realistic value ( $u_{0}=80$ meV), the Berry curvature becomes increasingly concentrated near $\Gamma$ , as seen from the line cuts in Fig. 4(a). In parallel, $A_{t}(\Gamma,\omega)$ develops an increasingly pronounced peak at $\omega=0$ in Fig.4 (b). The full electron and trion spectra in Fig.4 (c-h) show the same trend, with the electron and trion developing a more sharply defined low-energy Dirac-like feature near $\Gamma$ . This quantitative correspondence supports that Dirac trions arise from the combined effect of concentrated topology and strong Coulomb interactions.

Discussion.- In this work we systematically investigated the Dirac trion excitation in magic angle twisted bilayer graphene. Through sign problem free QMC, we showed that these trions are the elementary charged excitations in the Mott semimetal normal state. Furthermore, we verified that these low energy trions are exactly orthogonal to the electron. These bound states are highly dispersive, arbitrarily light near the magic angle, despite being composed of electrons and holes from the heavy parts of the band. These properties are unique amongst many-body excitations to our knowledge. Their emergence from the flat bands of twisted bilayer graphene, with concentrated charge density and Berry curvature, demonstrates that new exotic excitations can emerge from strongly correlated topological bands beyond Landau levels. We expect our computational techniques to be applicable and influential to future investigations in this timely direction.

Our computational demonstration of Dirac trions in the Bistritzer-Macdonald model suggests that these excitations are fundamental to realistic magic angle graphene. Indeed, a recent [105] quantum twisting microscope (QTM) [43, 101] study finds low electron spectral weight, and no electron Fermi surface, when doping integer filling states away from charge neutrality — precisely where a light trion Fermi surface is expected theoretically. Future QTM experiments could provide indirect evidence for trions at neutrality by scanning low-strain samples[44, 93] with slowly varying twist angle and observing the evolution of the electron spectral function. More direct detection of trions may also be possible through phonon or photon assisted tunneling, as while the trion does not overlap with any single electron, it does overlap with electrons bound to particle-hole pairs.

Supplemental Material for “Trion Excitations in Twisted Bilayer Graphene: a Quantum Monte Carlo Study”

Shibo Shan, Cheng Huang, Patrick Ledwith and Zi Yang Meng

In this Supplemental Material, we provide technical details for the trion operator construction and QMC measurement of the trion Green’s function. In Sec. S1, we construct the trion operator by introducing the AA-centered Wannier-like orbital used in the trion and explain its relation to the local charge channel of the projected interaction. In Sec. S2, we describe the evaluation of the trion Green’s function in momentum-space QMC, emphasizing the reduction of the computational cost in the QMC measurement from the direct momentum-space Wick expansion to the real-space implementation. In Sec. S3, we summarize the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm used for global auxiliary-field updates.

## S1 construction of the Trion operator

As discussed in the main text, we define the trion operator as

$$ F_{\mathbf{k}\sigma s\eta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{R}}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\bigl\{c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta},\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}\bigr\}, $$

with

$$ c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in{\rm mBZ}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}c_{\mathbf{k}\sigma s\eta},\qquad\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}=\sum_{\sigma,s,\eta}c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}-4. $$

Here $s$ and $\eta$ denote spin and valley, $\sigma=\pm$ labels the sublattice-polarized (Chern) basis within the two BM flat bands [12]. This basis is introduced so that the Fourier-transformed operator $c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}$ creates a projected orbital localized near the AA region of the moiré unit cell. In this case, $\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}$ can be interpreted as the local charge fluctuation, making $\{c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta},\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}\}$ the natural Hubbard-like local trion operator.

To construct this basis, we rotate the two BM energy bands at each $\mathbf{k}$ by diagonalizing the projected sublattice operator

$$ \Gamma_{nn^{\prime}}^{\eta}(\mathbf{k})=\langle u_{n\eta}(\mathbf{k})|\sigma_{z}|u_{n^{\prime}\eta}(\mathbf{k})\rangle, $$

and define

$$ c_{\mathbf{k}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}=\sum_{n}X_{\sigma n}^{\eta}(\mathbf{k})c_{\mathbf{k}ns\eta}^{\dagger}, $$

where $|u_{n\eta}({\mathbf{k}})\rangle$ is the eigenvector of BM Hamiltonian, $\sigma_{z}$ acts on the microscopic graphene sublattice, and $X_{\sigma n}^{\eta}(\mathbf{k})$ are the eigenvectors of $\Gamma^{\eta}(\mathbf{k})$ . To make $c_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}$ create an AA-centered orbital, we multiply each eigenvector by a phase factor $\chi_{\mathbf{k}\sigma}^{\eta}$ , chosen such that the top-layer $A$ -sublattice component of the resulting Bloch spinor created by $c_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}$ is real and positive at the AA center. At the $\Gamma$ point this top-layer $A$ -sublattice component vanishes, $c_{\Gamma\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}$ cannot create a Bloch function concentrated at the AA center, so we exclude its contribution by setting $X_{\sigma n}^{\eta}(\Gamma)=0$ in the trion operator. This gauge choice ensures that the real-space wavefunction created by $c_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}$

$$ w_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}^{\alpha l}(\mathbf{r})=\langle\mathbf{r},\alpha,l|c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}^{\dagger}|0\rangle $$

has a charge profile

$$ \rho_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\alpha,l}\left|w_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta}^{\alpha l}(\mathbf{r})\right|^{2} $$

The charge profiles are concentrated near the AA center, supporting the use of $\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}$ as a local AA charge fluctuation in the trion operator.*

The above construction expresses the intrinsic AA concentration of the flat-band wave functions in an AA-centered projected orbital basis. In this basis, $\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}$ measures the local AA charge fluctuation associated with the leading Hubbard-like component of the projected interaction. Thus $\{c_{\mathbf{R}\sigma s\eta},\delta n_{\mathbf{R}}\}$ is the projected analogue of the local Hubbard trion operator.

## S2 Measurement of the Trion operator in QMC

In this section, we discuss the QMC measurement of the trion Green’s function $G_{FF}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)$ . For each auxiliary-field configuration $\phi$ , the fermionic problem is quadratic. We define the corresponding time-ordered single-particle Green’s function as

$$ \displaystyle G_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}n_{1};{\mathbf{k}}_{2}n_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})={\left\langle\mathcal{T}_{\tau}c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}n_{1}s\eta}(\tau_{1})c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{2}n_{2}s\eta}^{\dagger}(\tau_{2})\right\rangle}_{\phi} $$

which is directly computed in the QMC simulation [113, 39]. $\mathcal{T}_{\tau}$ is the imaginary-time-ordering operator and $\langle\cdots\rangle_{\phi}$ denotes the fermionic value evaluated for a specific auxiliary-field configuration $\phi$ . Note that Eq. (S7) adopts an auxiliary-field contraction convention without the conventional overall minus sign used for the physical fermionic Green’s functions in the main text. For equal-time contractions, we use the one-sided convention $G(\tau,\tau)\equiv\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0^{+}}G(\tau+\epsilon,\tau).$ Then, the expectation value of observables $\langle O\rangle$ can be obtained by first evaluating the Wick-expanded estimator $\langle O\rangle_{\phi}$ for a fixed $\phi$ , and then averaging the estimator over the Monte Carlo ensemble of auxiliary-field configurations as $\langle O\rangle=\frac{1}{N_{\phi}}\sum_{\phi}\langle O\rangle_{\phi}$ . For notational simplicity, in the following we suppress the auxiliary-field label $\phi$ and leave the Monte Carlo average over auxiliary-field configurations implicit.

In $\mathbf{k}$ space basis we write Eq. (S1) with imaginary time $\tau$ dependence explicitly as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} F_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma s\eta}(\tau)&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}{\mathbf{k}}_{2}{\mathbf{k}}_{3}\sigma_{1}s_{1}\eta_{1}}\delta_{{\mathbf{k}}+{\mathbf{k}}_{1}-{\mathbf{k}}_{2}-{\mathbf{k}}_{3}={\mathbf{G}}}\{c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{3}\sigma s\eta}(\tau),\,c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}\sigma_{1}s_{1}\eta_{1}}^{\dagger}(\tau)c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{2}\sigma_{1}s_{1}\eta_{1}}(\tau)\}-8\,c_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma s\eta}(\tau)\end{aligned} $$

We then compute the trion Green’s function as $[G_{FF}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)]_{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}=-\langle F_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma_{1}s\eta}(\tau)F_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma_{2}s\eta}^{\dagger}(0)\rangle$ . It is evaluated by Wick expansion as products of sublattice-polarized basis Green’s functions $G_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}\sigma_{1};{\mathbf{k}}_{2}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ , which is obtained from the band-basis Green’s function measured in QMC as

$$ G_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}\sigma_{1};{\mathbf{k}}_{2}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=\sum_{n_{1},n_{2}}X_{\sigma_{1}n_{1}}^{\eta*}({\mathbf{k}}_{1})X_{\sigma_{2}n_{2}}^{\eta}({\mathbf{k}}_{2})G_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}n_{1};{\mathbf{k}}_{2}n_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}), $$

A direct momentum-space evaluation contains four independent internal momentum sums in $G_{FF}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)$ , leading to an $O(N^{4})$ cost for each fixed $({\mathbf{k}},\tau)$ . This is even higher than the computational complexity of the global QMC update of $O(N^{3})$ and becomes a bottleneck that severely limits the system sizes accessible and, therefore, limits the momentum resolution of the trion spectra.

To overcome this problem in the trion Green’s function measurement, we change the basis of the two-point Green’s functions from momentum space into real space in the moiré scale $\mathbf{R}$ to reduce the computation complexity. From Eq. (S1) we have

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} F_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma s\eta}(\tau)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma^{\prime}s^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}}e^{-i{\mathbf{k}}\cdot{\mathbf{R}}}\Big(\{c_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma s\eta}(\tau),\ c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma^{\prime}s^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}}(\tau)c_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma^{\prime}s^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}}(\tau)\}-c_{{\mathbf{R}}\sigma s\eta}(\tau)\Big)\end{aligned} $$

Then the trion Green’s function takes the form

$$ [G_{FF}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)]^{s\eta}_{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}=-\langle F_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma_{1}s\eta}(\tau)F_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma_{2}s\eta}^{\dagger}(0)\rangle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\mathbf{R}}_{1}\sigma^{\prime}_{1}s^{\prime}_{1}\eta^{\prime}_{1}\\
{\mathbf{R}}_{2}\sigma_{2}^{\prime}s^{\prime}_{2}\eta^{\prime}_{2}\end{subarray}}e^{i{\mathbf{k}}\cdot({\mathbf{R}}_{2}-{\mathbf{R}}_{1})}\langle O\rangle $$

where

$$ \langle O\rangle\equiv-\langle\big(\{c_{{\mathbf{R}}_{1}\sigma_{1}{\mathrm{s}}\eta}(\tau),\,c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{R}}_{1}\sigma_{1}^{\prime}s_{1}^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}_{1}}(\tau)c_{{\mathbf{R}}_{1}\sigma_{1}^{\prime}s_{1}^{\prime}\eta_{1}^{\prime}}(\tau)\}-c_{{\mathbf{R}}_{1}\sigma_{1}s\eta}(\tau)\big)\big(\{c_{{\mathbf{R}}_{2}\sigma_{2}{\mathrm{s}}\eta}^{\dagger}(0),\,c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{R}}_{2}\sigma_{2}^{\prime}s_{2}^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}_{2}}(0)c_{{\mathbf{R}}_{2}\sigma_{2}^{\prime}s_{2}^{\prime}\eta_{2}^{\prime}}(0)\}-c_{{\mathbf{R}}_{2}\sigma_{2}s\eta}^{\dagger}(0)\big)\rangle. $$

We then evaluate the term $\langle O\rangle$ as combinations of $G_{{\mathbf{R}}_{1}\sigma_{1};{\mathbf{R}}_{2}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ by Wick expansion, where

$$ G_{{\mathbf{R}}_{1}\sigma_{1};{\mathbf{R}}_{2}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1},{\mathbf{k}}_{2}}e^{i({\mathbf{k}}_{1}\cdot{\mathbf{R}}_{1}-{\mathbf{k}}_{2}\cdot{\mathbf{R}}_{2})}G_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}\sigma_{1};{\mathbf{k}}_{2}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}). $$

We evaluate this double Fourier transform using the fast Fourier transform (FFT) algorithm [19], which has a computational complexity of $O(N^{2}\log(N))$ . By evaluating the trion Green’s function through Eq. (S11), we successfully reduce the 4 independent momentum loops to the 2 moiré unit cell ${\mathbf{R}}$ loops, with a computational complexity of $O(N^{2})$ . The Wick expansion of the term $\langle O\rangle$ is evaluated as $\langle O\rangle=\sum_{i}a_{i}G_{i1}G_{i2}G_{i3}$ , where $a_{i}$ , $G_{i1}$ , $G_{i2}$ , and $G_{i3}$ are listed in the Table S1. The convention $X(\Gamma)=0$ in the trion operator construction changes the anticommutator of the real-space electron operators to

$$ \{c_{\mathbf{R}a},c_{\mathbf{R}^{\prime}b}^{\dagger}\}=\left(\delta_{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{N}\right)\delta_{ab},\qquad a,b=(\sigma,s,\eta). $$

Therefore the explicit delta factors in the coefficient $a_{i}$ of Table S1 should be read as

$$ \delta_{x_{2},y_{2}}\rightarrow(1-1/N)\delta_{\sigma_{2}\sigma_{2}^{\prime}}\delta_{ss_{2}^{\prime}}\delta_{\eta\eta_{2}^{\prime}},\qquad\delta_{y_{1},x_{1}}\rightarrow(1-1/N)\delta_{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{1}^{\prime}}\delta_{ss_{1}^{\prime}}\delta_{\eta\eta_{1}^{\prime}}. $$

By contrast, other observables such as $[G_{cc}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)]_{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}$ or $[G_{cF}({\mathbf{k}},\tau)]_{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}$ are still evaluated directly in momentum space by Wick expanding them in terms of $G_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}\sigma_{1};{\mathbf{k}}_{2}\sigma_{2}}^{s\eta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ .

## S3 Metropolis-Adjusted Langevin Sampling of the Auxiliary Fields

In this section, we describe the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA) proposal used to sample the Hubbard–Stratonovich auxiliary fields in our momentum-space determinant QMC simulation. After the Hubbard–Stratonovich decoupling of the density-density interaction, the auxiliary-field configuration $\phi\equiv\{\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},1},\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},2}\}$ is sampled from the probability distribution function [40]

$$ \pi(\phi)\propto e^{-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{{\mathbf{Q}}\in\text{half}}(\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},1}^{2}+\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},2}^{2})}\text{Tr}_{f}(\prod_{\tau}e^{i\sum_{{\mathbf{Q}}\in\text{half}}(-\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},1}\sqrt{\alpha_{2}({\mathbf{Q}})}A_{\mathbf{Q}}+i\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},2}\sqrt{\alpha_{2}({\mathbf{Q}})}B_{{\mathbf{Q}}})}e^{-\Delta\tau H_{0}}) $$

where ${\mathbf{Q}}={\mathbf{q}}+{\mathbf{G}}$ , $A_{\mathbf{Q}}=\delta\rho_{-{\mathbf{Q}}}+\delta\rho_{{\mathbf{Q}}}$ , $B_{{\mathbf{Q}}}=\delta\rho_{-{\mathbf{Q}}}-\delta\rho_{{\mathbf{Q}}}$ , $\alpha_{2}({\mathbf{Q}})=\Delta\tau V({\mathbf{Q}})/2\Omega$ . The definition of $\delta\rho_{\mathbf{Q}}$ is given in the main text. The notation $\sum_{{\mathbf{Q}}\in\text{half}}$ means that only one momentum from each pair $\pm{\mathbf{Q}}$ is included. At charge neutrality, the $C_{2}P$ symmetry relates the two valleys and guarantees the absence of the fermion sign problem [113]. The MALA proposal uses the local gradient of the logarithmic probability distribution. For a collective index $i\equiv(\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},a)$ , with $a=1,2$ , a new auxiliary-field configuration is proposed according to [30]

$$ \phi_{i}^{\prime}=\phi_{i}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\frac{\partial\ln(\pi(\phi))}{\partial\phi_{i}}+\sigma\xi_{i} $$

where each $\xi_{i}$ is independently drawn from a standard normal distribution. The parameter $\sigma$ controls the step size of the global proposal. In practice, we tune $\sigma$ such that the acceptance ratio is close to the optimal high-dimensional MALA value $0.574$ [82]. The proposed configuration is accepted with probability

$$ P(\phi\rightarrow\phi^{\prime})=\text{min}(1,\frac{\pi(\phi^{\prime})q(\phi|\phi^{\prime})}{\pi(\phi)q(\phi^{\prime}|\phi)}) $$

where

$$ q(\phi^{\prime}|\phi)\propto\text{exp}\Big(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{i}\Big(\phi_{i}^{\prime}-\phi_{i}-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\frac{\partial\ln\pi(\phi)}{\partial\phi_{i}}\Big)^{2}\Big) $$

We calculate $\frac{\partial\ln(\pi(\phi))}{\partial\phi_{i}}$ as

$$ \frac{\partial\ln\pi(\phi)}{\partial\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},1}}=-\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},1}+4\sqrt{\alpha_{2}({\mathbf{Q}})}\,\mathrm{Im}\left\{\mathrm{Tr}\left[\left(I-G^{s\eta}(\tau,\tau)\right)\mathcal{A}_{{\mathbf{Q}}}^{s\eta}\right]\right\}, $$

and

$$ \frac{\partial\ln\pi(\phi)}{\partial\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},2}}=-\phi_{\tau,{\mathbf{Q}},2}-4\sqrt{\alpha_{2}({\mathbf{Q}})}\,\mathrm{Re}\left\{\mathrm{Tr}\left[\left(I-G^{s\eta}(\tau,\tau)\right)\mathcal{B}_{{\mathbf{Q}}}^{s\eta}\right]\right\}. $$

Here $G^{s\eta}(\tau,\tau)$ is the equal-time single-particle Green’s function matrix in the $({\mathbf{k}},m)$ basis,

$$ [G^{s\eta}(\tau,\tau)]_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}m_{1};{\mathbf{k}}_{2}m_{2}}=\left\langle c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}m_{1}s\eta}(\tau)c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{2}m_{2}s\eta}^{\dagger}(\tau)\right\rangle_{\phi}. $$

The matrices $\mathcal{A}_{{\mathbf{Q}}}^{s\eta}$ and $\mathcal{B}_{{\mathbf{Q}}}^{s\eta}$ are the single-particle matrix representations of $A_{{\mathbf{Q}}}$ and $B_{{\mathbf{Q}}}$ , with constant terms omitted. Equivalently, their matrix elements are the coefficients of $c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{1}m_{1}s\eta}^{\dagger}c_{{\mathbf{k}}_{2}m_{2}s\eta}$ in the corresponding bilinear operators.
